solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Assume the setter’s optimistic?

blocks.note: to posit is to assume or put forward as fact
the setter says 'I', so 'the setter has' is I'VE

explanation.surface: A solver asks whether the setter is taking an upbeat view of things.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as 'is', but here it stands for 'has': the setter has = I've, giving POSIT + I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone positive expects good outcomes and looks on the bright side, which is being hopeful.

clue.text: Quietly mentions compliments

blocks.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quietly
to raise a point is to mention it

explanation.surface: Someone murmurs a few flattering remarks under their breath.
explanation.walkthrough: P for quietly comes from music notation, where piano means soft.
explanation.definitionFit: Praises and compliments are both plural nouns for admiring remarks expressing approval of someone.

clue.text: Aggrieved about hotel in coastal area

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: sore can mean resentful or aggrieved
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A guest is annoyed about the hotel they stayed at by the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: SORE wraps around H.
explanation.definitionFit: The shore is the strip of land bordering the sea, the edge of any coast.

clue.text: Maybe film exotic vale route, Greece’s first?

indicators.note: something exotic is strange and foreign, so these letters take an unfamiliar arrangement
the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
the opening letter of Greece

explanation.surface: A documentary might follow a picturesque valley road through Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' flags that a film is only one example of the answer, which can also be a book or talk.
explanation.definitionFit: A travelogue is a film, lecture or book describing a journey and the places visited, so a film is one example.

clue.text: Initially very edgy, lets visitor examine tendentious material

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives up its opening letter

blocks.clueFragment: very edgy, lets visitor examine tendentious
blocks.note: the opening letters of these six words

explanation.surface: A nervous host allows a guest to look over some biased documents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Material' looks like the documents being examined, but it is the definition, meaning fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Velvet is a soft fabric with a dense pile, a kind of cloth or textile.

clue.text: Good boy is happy

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A well-behaved child is a cheerful one.
explanation.walkthrough: G for good is a common crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Glad and happy are simple synonyms for feeling pleased or cheerful.

clue.text: One spotted sign of expected standard on top of door?

indicators.note: in a down answer, one piece sitting on another means it comes directly above it
the top of a word in a down answer is its first letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: Leo is a sign of the zodiac
par is the expected or normal standard, as in golf
the first letter of door

explanation.surface: Someone notices a mark showing the required quality on a door frame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One spotted' reads as 'someone noticed', but it means an animal with spots.
explanation.definitionFit: The leopard is a big cat famous for its spotted coat, hence a creature covered in spots.

clue.text: Parent penning note — that’s unfashionable

indicators.note: to pen something is to shut it in, as animals in a pen, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: a dad is a parent
te is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A child complains that a parent writing a letter is behind the times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning' suggests writing, but it means enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dated belongs to an earlier time and now seems old-fashioned or out of style.

clue.text: Charming commercial to cheer finally — clever

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so each word keeps only its closing letter

blocks.note: an ad is a commercial
the closing letters of both words
able means capable or clever

explanation.surface: A viewer praises a delightful advert that ends on an upbeat, witty note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' applies to both 'to' and 'cheer', not just the nearer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Adorable and charming both describe someone or something delightful and very easy to like.

clue.text: Memo attached showing defensive feature

indicators.note: showing means on display, so the letters are visible within the words themselves

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: An office memo comes with a note about the building's safety measures.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'meMO ATtached'.
explanation.definitionFit: A moat is a water-filled ditch dug around a castle to keep attackers out.

clue.text: Collection of quips maybe about cheeky Oscar — anger follows

indicators.note: to follow is to come after, so this piece is placed at the end

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
pert means cheeky or saucy
O is Oscar in the NATO phonetic alphabet
ire is anger

explanation.surface: A comic's stock of jokes about an impudent Oscar Wilde gets someone cross.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' flags that quips are only one kind of thing a performer can have a stock of.
explanation.definitionFit: A repertoire is the full range of pieces, songs or jokes a performer is ready to deliver.

clue.text: National vegetable

blocks.note: first meaning
second meaning: a large yellow-fleshed root, called rutabaga in North America

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read as one phrase, a country's signature vegetable, but they are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A national is a citizen of a country, and a Swede is a citizen of Sweden; the swede is also a turnip-like root crop.

clue.text: Mere lad potentially a gem?

indicators.note: potentially means what something could become, so the letters could be rearranged into something else

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a mere boy might turn out to be a treasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A gem' also means a wonderful person, which is why the lad fits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An emerald is a precious green stone, one of the classic jewels.

clue.text: Programme cost I’m working out

indicators.note: working something out means processing and reorganising it, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A producer is calculating the budget for a TV show.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'I'm' is ignored, leaving the letters I and M.
explanation.definitionFit: A sitcom, or situation comedy, is a type of television or radio show.

clue.text: Be of use after right upset in Labour?

indicators.note: upset means turned over, and in a down answer that turns the letters back to front
one piece coming after another sets the order in which they are joined

blocks.note: RT is an abbreviation for right
to avail is to be of use or benefit

explanation.surface: A voter wonders whether a right-wing shock could help the Labour Party.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital L makes 'Labour' look like the British political party; it is hard work.
explanation.definitionFit: Travail is an old word for painful, strenuous effort, including the labour of childbirth.

clue.text: Dull scenes essentially fronted by principal actor

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so only the central letters are kept
being fronted by something means having it placed in front, which sets the order

blocks.note: the lead is the main actor in a production
the two central letters of the six-letter word

explanation.surface: A critic complains that a play's boring scenes are dominated by its star.
explanation.walkthrough: With six letters, the middle of 'scenes' is its third and fourth letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaden literally means made of lead, and figuratively heavy, sluggish and lifeless.

clue.text: Growth area in North Surrey refurbished

indicators.note: something refurbished has been done up and remade, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for north
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A developing district in the north of Surrey, an English county near London, has been done up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Growth area' sounds like economic development, but it is a place where plants are grown.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant nursery is where young plants and trees are raised for sale or planting.

clue.text: No opening for beginner as breadwinner

indicators.note: with no opening, a word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a learner is a beginner

explanation.surface: A newcomer finds no job openings to support the family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No opening' suggests a lack of jobs, but it removes the first letter, L.
explanation.definitionFit: A breadwinner is the person who earns money to support a household.

clue.text: Something in kitchen quarrel you heard? “Not half lazy!”

indicators.note: something heard is taken by ear, so the sound counts rather than the spelling
not half means half is removed, so only one half of the word remains

blocks.note: a spat is a petty quarrel
the letter U is pronounced like the word you
taken as written, then cut in half

explanation.surface: During a row in the kitchen, someone calls another bone idle.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing half of LAZY leaves LA.
explanation.definitionFit: A spatula is a flat-bladed utensil for lifting, turning or spreading food while cooking.

clue.text: Dish, second, our people welcome

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
us refers to ourselves
hi is a greeting of welcome

explanation.surface: A host serves a second course that the family greets warmly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welcome' looks like a verb but gives the greeting HI.
explanation.definitionFit: Sushi is a Japanese preparation of vinegared rice with raw fish, served as a meal or course.

clue.text: On return, did exam second time? That could be stunning

indicators.note: a return is a journey back, so the letters are read the other way

blocks.note: to resit an exam is to take it again

explanation.surface: A student back from a trip retakes a test and hopes the result will be brilliant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stunning' suggests an outstanding result, but it means delivering an electric shock.
explanation.definitionFit: A Taser is a weapon that fires electrified darts to incapacitate a person with a shock.

clue.text: For listeners, remained formal

indicators.note: listeners take in sound, so the word is identified by how it is spoken

blocks.note: remained means stayed

explanation.surface: An audience notes that someone kept things strictly proper.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words of the same pronunciation: the past tense of stay and an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Staid describes someone sedate, respectable and unadventurous, stiffly correct in manner.

clue.text: Items robbed from Devon maybe, silver

blocks.note: Devon, an English county, lies in the South West, abbreviated SW
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: Burglars in Devon make off with the family silver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' flags Devon as one example of a region in the South West of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Swag is slang for stolen goods, the loot carried off by thieves.

clue.text: Secret hint

blocks.note: first meaning, an adjective: private and personal
second meaning, a verb: to suggest indirectly

explanation.walkthrough: The two meanings are pronounced differently: the adjective ends in -mut, the verb in -mate.
explanation.definitionFit: Intimate details are private and confidential, while to intimate something is to imply it indirectly.

clue.text: Change in deli not working

indicators.note: to change something is to alter its form, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A customer notes the delicatessen's till isn't giving out coins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' looks like coins in the till, but it tells you to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine or person that is idle is inactive, doing nothing, out of action.

clue.text: Like some matches after Friday finish, extremely lively

indicators.note: one piece coming after another fixes the order in which they are joined
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its outer letters are kept

blocks.note: the first three letters of Friday, its usual short form on calendars
an end is a finish
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Games played after the working week ends on Friday are full of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: A friendly is a sports fixture played for no competitive stake, so some matches are friendly.
explanation.definitionFit: A friendly match is an unofficial game where nothing like league points or a trophy is at stake.
